newsitem.title: FRANCE: French insurer Axa's profits jump pre-merger.
newsitem.headline: French insurer Axa's profits jump pre-merger.

text.p: Axa, which is merging with rival French group UAP to create the world's second largest insurer, on Wednesday said 1996 profits rocketed 40 percent.

Axa's net attributable profit soared to 3.81 billion francs ($670 million) from 2.73 billion on revenues up 28 percent to 167.21 billion. It boosted its dividend 15.4 percent to 7.50 francs. Earnings per share rose 20.8 percent to 20.36 francs.

Clearing the decks for the merger, UAP reported a loss of 6.45 billion francs after writing off 7.59 billion francs in one-off charges to purge its books and prevent money-losing activities weighing on the new group's future.

Stripping out the one-off charges -- which included cover for businesses in a collapsed property sector as well as the deconsolidation of French bank BNP in its accounts -- UAP's profit was 1.14 billion francs. Union des Assurances de Paris had a net attributable loss of 2.1 billion francs in 1995.
"UAP is a good company which probably made investments that were a little risky in the past," Axa chairman Claude Bebear, who will head the new group, told reporters.
"We have taken the last necessary provisions to erase what was done in the past," he said, expressing confidence about the merged company's future. "Things are going well."

Axa and UAP, France's two largest insurers, are integrating their operations to form Axa-UAP after surprising financial markets last November with the news that they would combine to create a French heavyweight in the global insurance business. The group will be known commercially worldwide as Axa.
Wednesday was the last time Axa and UAP will produce separate accounts. From this year their figures will be consolidated. Shareholders are due to vote on the merger in May.

Axa, widely regarded as the best quality player in the French insurance sector and the driving force of the new duo, said the merged group would aim for average growth of 15 percent a year in net profit per share between 1996 and 2000.

Bebear, credited with pulling off the merger, said the new group would seek return on equity -- a key measure of corporate performance -- of 15 percent "at the start of the next century" and of "at least 11 percent" in 1998. Axa had return on equity of 10.2 percent in 1996 and 8.5 percent in 1995.

Asked about his own plans, Bebear, who turns 62 in July, said 65 was a "reasonable age" to retire but did not commit himself. He is believed to want to oversee and consolidate the merger which marks the pinnacle of a career that has taken him from a small Normandy mutal company to heading a global player.
One analyst said the main challenge facing the group was to boost its return on equity (ROE) to U.S. levels but believed it would be done. U.S. insurers' ROE is 16 to 17 percent, he said.
Axa said its performance was powered by life insurance, due to a big improvement in the United States, France and Britain.
Axa shares closed up 1.03 percent at 371.80 francs. Analysts said the figures, flagged beforehand, contained no surprises.

Axa's profits were also lifted by property and casualty insurance results which increased strongly in France, Belgium and Britain. The exception was Axa Global Risks in Britain which had losses due to strengthening of reserves for pre-1992 claims.
First-time full-year consolidation of life insurer National Mutual in Australia, whose 1995 acquisition was seen as giving Axa a springboard for Asia, also helped drive profits.

There was a hefty increase in income from U.S. financial services -- DLJ and Alliance Capital Management -- and a robust contribution from the holding company thanks to "very good investment results." Its holding had a profit of 148 million francs against a loss of 248 million the previous year.
But some downward pressure on profits came from losses at the Axa Leben life insurance unit in Germany and at French real estate subsidiaries due to real estate valuation allowances.
